newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Erbakan boosted ahead of censure motion.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Erbakan boosted ahead of censure motion.

text.p: Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan got a morale boost from his party faithful at a triumphalist congress on Sunday ahead of a parliamentary challenge this week to his brief tenure as modern Turkey's first Islamist leader.
"This government will work in harmony until the year 2000," Erbakan said in a speech to a cheering crowd of 10,000 Welfare Party supporters in a packed sports hall.
He was welcomed to the podium by the strains of military marches played by a traditional Ottoman band. Followers waved red-and-white party flags and hand-held "sparkler" fireworks.
Erbakan, in a 90-minute speech, only briefly touched on an opposition censure motion he faces in parliament on Wednesday for a disastrous trip to Libya eight days ago.
"Why have they given a censure motion?" he asked. "They don't want peace at home and abroad, they want a fight."
The Libya trip exposed Turkey to criticism from both his hosts and Ankara's NATO ally Washington. It badly damaged his plans to take Turkey closer to the Moslem and Arab world.
Erbakan denied he was attempting to steer Moslem but secular Turkey away from the West.
"Turkey is carrying out its own individual foreign policy. We are not changing tack or anything like that," he said.

The opposition have accused Erbakan of bringing Turkey into disrepute with his Libya visit, during which Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi slammed Ankara for its treatment of the Kurds and its close ties to the West.
Parliament will debate and vote on Wednesday whether to go ahead with the censure motion. Erbakan would have to resign if the motion was approved by the 550-seat assembly.
On paper, Erbakan has the backing of 281 MPs, five more than is needed to win the vote, but some members of partner Tansu Ciller's True Path Party (DYP) are uneasy with the Libya affair.

However, analysts say the vast majority of DYP MPs are likely to stick with Erbakan for fear of a return of the political chaos that deprived Turkey of steady leadership for nine months before Welfare formed a government in June.

Erbakan has so far failed in promises like solving a 12-year-old Kurdish rebel campaign through "Moslem brotherhood" while populist measures, like 50 percent wage rises for more than seven million civil servants, have burdened the shaky economy.
He vowed not to give into Kurdish demands for self rule, in hardline comments similar to those made by many of his secularist predecessor.
"We will protect the unitary status of the state," he said. "We will not permit arguments aimed at the security forces," Erbakan told his party.
Welfare, the most disciplined party in Turkey, looks to be firmly behind Erbakan after he snuffed out a leadership challenge to a provincial party boss close to him last month.
He was to be re-elected party leader, as the only candidate, later on Sunday.
